claims: Early: the brain is 12.5x more likely to believe a gesture over words, because it is very hard to lie with gestures; liars use fewer gestures.
Early: sitting within 25 ft of a high performer improves your own performance by 15%; confidence correlates with the distance between shoulder and earlobes.
Early: 82% of impressions of people are based on warmth and competence; five power cues for confidence, five warmth cues for approachability.
Middle: lower-lid flex is a power cue of focus that signals deep listening; it also reveals skepticism/confusion you should address before moving on.
Middle: vocal cues tell people how you feel about them and yourself; accidental question inflection (uptalk) flips the listener's brain from listening to scrutinizing.

Middle: in a two-truths-and-a-lie lab experiment, liars overwhelmingly asked their lie ('Do you believe this?'); salespeople's biggest mistake is asking their price with uptalk, signaling they don't believe the number.
Late: Monica Moore's attraction research: the people approached most were not the most attractive, but those with the biggest signal of availability.
Late: availability signals: open torso (nothing blocking), 'croissant feet' angled toward the room, short side glances; roughly eight glances can trigger an approach.
title: Body Language Expert: Stop Using This, It’s Making People Dislike You, So Are These Subtle Mistakes!

claims: Middle: 'tactical empathy' is the core system: deliberately demonstrating understanding of the other side's perspective.

Middle: labeling ('sounds like...', 'seems like...') names emotions to defuse them; mirroring (repeating 1-3 of the speaker's words) is the lowest-effort tool and recruits a different brain system than labeling.
Middle: long emails/texts almost always come off cold; soften hard messages instead of over-explaining.
Late: negotiation is collaboration, not battle; physical and mental stamina matter because real negotiations play out over days to months.
Late: probe questions (calibrated questions) reveal deception; watch for emotional incongruence, not just words.
title: How to Succeed at Hard Conversations | Chris Voss

claims: Early: a recent study found 95% of people have worked with someone who talks too much; nonverbal cues of checkout include the 'open fish' mouth cue.
Early: one in six people worldwide is affected by loneliness; a voice note is 'the most selfish form of conversation.'

Early: in three 500-person speed-networking experiments, the best conversation starter was 'What was the highlight of your day?'; the worst question in the history of conversations is 'What do you do?'

Middle: the conversation blueprint has three levels - general traits, personal concerns (motivations, goals, values, worries), then identity; skipping level one makes depth feel invasive, like an interrogation.
Middle: the mechanics of 'rizz': speaking turns longer than ~45 seconds create friction; conversational narcissists and autopilot questions ('How are you?') destroy connection.
Late: five story archetypes decode the psychological narratives people live in (e.g. the ambitious hero); body language has a 'maximum resonance point' that projects warmth and competence.
title: Vanessa Van Edwards: The Conversation Habit That Makes Smart People Unlikable

claims: Early: charisma defined as the ability to influence other people; there is not one style of charisma but several.
Early: nobody works on charisma, so a small amount of practice puts you in an elite tier ('if no one works out, the gym makes you exceptional fast').
Middle: courage is a muscle; shyness's 'I have nothing to say' is really an internal filter set too high - nothing passes the worthiness test.
Middle: progressive exposure therapy: say one extra sentence to a taxi driver, waiter, or cashier - start embarrassingly small.
Late: identity momentum: the behaviors you create become 'the creature that drags you along' - design the engine, then ride it.
title: You Can Become Socially Confident Pretty Quickly - Charlie Houpert

claims: Early/middle: social homeostasis - when you lack social interaction at your needed frequency/intensity, you crave it like hunger; mediated by unique dopamine neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN).
Middle: dopamine is not the 'feeling good' chemical; it is the neurochemical of movement toward things that feel good.
Middle: social hierarchies are plastic and dynamic; the brain continuously places you in a hierarchy and adjusts.
Middle: introversion/extroversion map onto different social-drive circuitry and dopamine responses, not just personality style.

Late: shared experiences that produce similar physiological states in two people merge physiologies and accelerate bonding; childhood attachment patterns show up as autonomic vs intellectual attachment in adulthood; emotional empathy vs cognitive empathy.
title: Science of Social Bonding in Family, Friendship & Romantic Love

claims: Early: the amygdala, famous for fear/threat detection, is actually involved in reinforcing positive, rewarding experiences.

Early: discovery of 'loneliness neurons' that fire when social interaction is unfulfilling, and of social homeostasis - the sense of getting enough/not enough social interaction regardless of introversion or extroversion.
Middle: animals and people sort into alphas/betas, dominants/subordinates in social hierarchies; rank shapes behavior and stress.
Middle: heavy social media interaction can leave people feeling specifically deprived - online contact does not satisfy the same circuits.
Late: the neurochemical and hormonal architecture of social interaction - what makes some interactions energizing and others depleting.
title: The Biology of Social Interactions & Emotions | Dr. Kay Tye

claims: Early: newest research - ask for someone's advice, not their opinion: asking for an opinion gets you a critic, asking for advice gets you a partner who gives more constructive input.
Early: influence vs manipulation turns on intent and the seven principles working toward genuine assent, not trickery.
Middle: the seven principles - reciprocation, liking, social proof, authority, scarcity, commitment & consistency, unity - each with small, concrete applications.
Late: how the principles combine and how to defend against them when used against you.
title: The Influence Expert: 7 Ways to Get People to Do What You Want (Even When They Don't Want To)

claims: Early: time is your only real possession - your 'empire' and 'treasure'; working for people you hate means they own it.
Early: win through your actions, not argument - demonstrate, don't explicate.
Middle: cultivate 'negative capability': develop the habit of suspending the need to judge everything; entertain viewpoints opposite to your own.
Middle: remake yourself into a character of power - sculpting yourself like clay is one of life's greatest tasks.
Late: do not be the court cynic - the ability to express wonder and amazement, and seem like you mean it, is a rare and dying talent, still greatly valued.
title: 12 Laws Of Power For Life - Robert Greene | Modern Wisdom Podcast 383

claims: Early: communication is not natural - the best communicators studied it as a skill set; anyone can become a 'supercommunicator' by practicing deliberate skills.

Early: every conversation is one of three kinds - practical (solving problems), emotional (share feelings, want empathy not solutions), social (relating to each other and society); two people having different kinds at once is why conversations fail.
Middle: consistent supercommunicators ask 10-20x more questions than the average person, including small invitations like 'what did you make of that?'

Middle: 'looping for understanding' - ask a deep question, listen, then repeat back in your own words (not mimicry), then ask 'did I get that right?'; proving you listened triggers reciprocity, making them listen back.
Late: in a good conversation, bodies match without noticing - breathing rate, heart rate, and pupil dilation mirror each other.
title: The Invisible Rules Of Social Success You Were Never Taught - Charles Duhigg

claims: Early: no one wants to hear anything you say unless you give them a reason to listen; telling a story is saying 'here's my humanity - what do you think of it?'

Early: anecdotes are cotton candy - delicious in the moment, instantly forgotten. Stories are the best meals of your life - remembered and reflected on for days, weeks, or a lifetime, because they connect to an emotion.
Early: most people don't tell stories, they report on their life chronologically ('some stuff happened and now I'm telling you') - that is not a story.
Middle: the most important decision is structure. The BABC model: start in the middle of the story instead of chronological ABC - opening with the ending gives away the outcome and kills curiosity.
Middle: turn 'and' stories into 'but/therefore' stories - conflict and causation structure (the South Park technique) is what makes a story engage.
title: How to Become a Master Storyteller (What Nobody Teaches You!)
